title: I released my cybersecurity tycoon game on Android today! Inspired by Game Dev Story and other classic tycoon games.
author: Hercull55
selftext:
After months of development, Cybersecurity Tycoon is finally available on Android! 🎉

It's a tycoon/management game inspired by classics like Game Dev Story, but focused on building and managing your own cybersecurity company.

You hire experts, complete contracts, research new technologies, expand your team, and grow your business from a small startup into a cybersecurity powerhouse.

The game is now available on both iOS and Android.

'd love to hear your feedback and answer any questions about the development process!

I used AI during the development of the game.

comments.author: Polyy-AI
comments.body: nice! How long did this project take you?

replies.author: Hercull55
replies.body:
Around 6 months from start to release!

The Android publishing process ended up taking a lot longer than I expected, and there were definitely a few moments where I wondered if I should keep going. 😅

But the feedback from my early testers was really encouraging. Seeing people enjoy the game, share suggestions, and ask for more content gave me the motivation to keep improving it and bring the project all the way to release.

replies.author: Lemonbicycle
replies.body:
Very very cool!

I played it and it is fun to play. There's a bunch of ui and ux notes, some audio and visual, but the mechanic works. Great job!

You are the first that I see here that published to the game store. I love that fact.

Can you share what other than the DUNS number was on your way, and why did you insist to go this path?

replies.author: Hercull55
replies.body:
Thanks a lot, I really appreciate that 

I actually didn’t have any major blocker on iOS. I published as an individual developer, so no DUNS or company setup issues in my case. The App Store side was pretty smooth overall since I’ve already published a few apps before.

The real challenge was more on the development side.

At some point, I seriously considered stopping the project, not because of publishing, but because I struggled to move the game from a prototype to something that felt like a “real product” balancing progression, improving UX, and dealing with pretty basic visuals at the time.

Apple wasn’t the issue at all (just a couple of small rejections around the in-app purchase / consumable setup, but nothing major).

Google Play was actually more painful in a different way the review/publishing process felt longer and more restrictive than expected, and that part almost made me drop the project.

What kept me going was early tester feedback. People were genuinely enjoying the core loop, even in its rough state, which gave me the motivation to finish it properly and push it to release.
